title: Global Youth Unemployment Rises as AI Threatens Millions of Entry-Level Jobs, ILO Warns
excerpt: The UN labor agency reports that 67 million young people were unemployed in 2025, reversing post-pandemic gains, while AI could displace 5.6 million more.
body:
• Global youth unemployment rose to 12.4 percent in 2025, reversing post-pandemic improvements, with 67 million people aged 15 to 24 out of work worldwide.
  • North America saw one of the sharpest increases, with youth unemployment climbing to 9.8 percent from 8.3 percent in 2023.
  • The ILO estimates 6.1 percent of jobs held by workers under 30 are highly exposed to AI, and if just 10 percent of those disappear, 5.6 million young workers could be displaced.
  • More than 257 million young people globally are not in employment, education or training, representing 20 percent of the youth population.

Global youth unemployment increased in 2025 as weaker economic growth, geopolitical tensions and sluggish job creation made it harder for young people to find work, the International Labour Organization said on Monday, warning that artificial intelligence could compound the pressure.

The global unemployment rate among 15-to-24-year-olds rose to 12.4 percent last year from 12.3 percent in 2023, equivalent to 67 million young people worldwide, according to the ILO's latest report. The increase reversed improvements recorded after the COVID-19 pandemic and reflected a deterioration in both the quantity and quality of available jobs.

A Near-Universal Decline

Youth unemployment worsened in eight of the world's 11 subregions between 2023 and 2025, the report found, with rates rising across high-income, lower-middle-income and low-income countries.

The Arab States recorded the highest youth unemployment rate at 26.2 percent, followed by Northern Africa at 22.6 percent. Some of the sharpest deterioration occurred in wealthier economies. Youth unemployment in North America climbed to 9.8 percent in 2025 from 8.3 percent in 2023. Across Northern, Southern and Western Europe, the rate stood at 15 percent.

The share of young people not in employment, education or training — known as NEET — also edged higher to 20 percent, representing more than 257 million people globally.

Middle-Skilled Jobs Disappearing

The ILO highlighted the decline of middle-skilled occupations — clerical, administrative, sales and manufacturing roles — that have traditionally served as entry points for young workers leaving school or university.

"A shrinkage of jobs associated with middle-skilled occupations means longer job queues and growing unemployment for young people with secondary-level education that seek them."

— ILO Global Employment Trends for Youth 2026 report

At the same time, jobs in high-skilled sectors such as science, engineering, healthcare and information technology continue to expand in most countries, creating a growing gap between the qualifications employers demand and those young workers hold.

AI Adds New Risk

The report warned that artificial intelligence could intensify the challenges facing young job seekers. The ILO estimated that 6.1 percent of jobs currently held by workers aged 15 to 29 are in occupations most exposed to AI-driven changes. If just 10 percent of those positions were eliminated entirely, around 5.6 million young workers — mainly in high-income countries — could face unemployment, forced career changes or exit from the labor force.

Preliminary evidence from the United States suggests that entry-level positions may be disproportionately affected by AI technologies, according to the report. Survey data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development shows younger, highly educated workers are more worried about AI-driven job losses than older workers who may be shielded by experience and seniority.

ILO Director-General Gilbert F. Houngbo called for coordinated action to address the trends.

"Unless governments, employers and workers act together to harness technology responsibly and expand quality job opportunities for women and youth, decent work deficits will persist and social cohesion will be at risk," Houngbo said, according to reporting by Reuters.

Informal Work Dominates in Poorer Countries

In developing economies, many young people cannot afford prolonged unemployment and instead take insecure, informal work. Nearly nine in 10 young workers in low- and lower-middle-income countries remain in informal employment, lacking adequate labor protections and social safety nets, the report found.

The ILO also noted that nearly 300 million workers globally are living in extreme poverty, earning less than three dollars a day. About 2.1 billion people are expected to work in the informal sector this year, with limited access to social protection and job security.

The overall global unemployment rate is projected to remain stable at around 4.9 percent in 2026, equivalent to some 186 million people out of work. But the ILO cautioned that headline stability masks deeper structural problems, including rising inequality, persistent gender gaps and the uneven reach of AI disruption across economies.
